content: Malaria continues to be a significant public health issue. Research conducted in the early 1900s suggested that modifying houses could potentially reduce malaria transmission. A previous review concluded that screening houses might be effective in reducing malaria. This updated review incorporates data from five new studies. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of house modifications designed to reduce mosquito exposure on malaria disease and its transmission. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CAB Abstracts, and LILACS, up to May 25, 2022. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through platforms such as the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the ISRCTN registry. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs), cross-over studies, and stepped-wedge designs. Quasi-experimental trials, such as controlled before-and-after studies, controlled interrupted time series, and non-randomized cross-over studies, were also eligible. The studies needed to investigate either primary construction or modifications to existing homes and report epidemiological outcomes, such as malaria case incidence, infection incidence, or parasite prevalence. Entomological outcomes, such as mosquito density, were also extracted if reported. Two authors independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Risk ratios (RR) were used to compare intervention effects for dichotomous data, while mean differences were used for continuous data. Rate ratios were applied for count and rate data. All results were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included one RCT and six cRCTs, with six additional RCTs still ongoing. All included studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa since 2009. Two trials randomized by household, while four randomized at the block or village level. The interventions primarily involved screening windows, doors, eaves, ceilings, or combinations of these. In some cases, these modifications were combined with roof alterations or the installation of eave tubes, which are insecticidal lure and kill devices designed to reduce mosquito entry while maintaining airflow. In one trial, the screening material was treated with 2% permethrin insecticide. In five trials, researchers implemented the interventions, while one trial adopted a community-based approach. The findings suggest that house modifications likely reduced malaria parasite prevalence (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.82; 5 trials, 5183 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, one study observed inconsistent effects in a subpopulation of children. House modifications also reduced the prevalence of moderate to severe anemia (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.89; 3 trials, 3643 participants; high-certainty evidence). There was no consistent effect on clinical malaria incidence, with rate ratios ranging from 0.38 to 1.62 (3 trials, 3365 participants, 4126.6 person-years). House modifications may reduce indoor mosquito density (rate ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.30; 4 trials, 9894 household-nights; low-certainty evidence), although two studies showed minimal impact on this parameter. In conclusion, house modifications, particularly screening, sometimes combined with insecticides or lure-and-kill devices, were associated with a reduction in malaria parasite prevalence and anemia prevalence. However, the findings on malaria incidence were inconsistent. Modifications were also linked to reduced indoor mosquito density, though this effect was not consistently observed across all studies.
